questions.prompt: In 'shift-left', what is being moved left on the project timeline?
options: Only the execution of automated UI tests
Testing activities and test thinking, so they start earlier (requirements, design, examples, reviews)
The release date
Production monitoring
questions.explanation: Shift-left means involving testing earlier in the lifecycle. It is not only about running UI tests sooner, and monitoring is a shift-right practice.

questions.prompt: Asking 'what should happen if the user enters a past date?' during backlog refinement is a shift-left activity.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Questioning a requirement before it is built is static testing at the earliest point, which is exactly what shift-left means.

questions.prompt: Which practice is a shift-right practice?
options: Reviewing acceptance criteria
Writing unit tests before code
Canary releases with production monitoring
Static analysis on every commit
questions.explanation: Canaries and monitoring learn from the live system, after release. The other three happen before or during development, so they are shift-left.

questions.prompt: Developers wait 70 minutes for pipeline feedback on every commit. Which stage ordering gives the fastest useful feedback?
options: UI end-to-end tests, then API tests, then unit tests, then linting
Linting and unit tests on commit; API/integration on merge; a small set of end-to-end and performance checks before release
Run everything in parallel on every commit and ignore duration
Remove automated tests and rely on manual regression
questions.explanation: Continuous testing layers checks so the fastest, cheapest ones run first and broad, slow ones run less often. Putting slow UI tests first delays all feedback; removing tests removes the safety net.

questions.prompt: A manual tester joins a story before any code exists. Which are useful shift-left contributions? Select all that apply.
options: Writing concrete examples for each acceptance criterion
Asking how errors and empty states should behave
Identifying test data and environment needs early
Waiting for the build so tests reflect the real UI
questions.explanation: Examples, questions about edge cases and early data/environment planning all prevent defects or delays. Waiting for the build is the opposite of shift-left.

questions.prompt: The pipeline fails about once a day for no clear reason and developers now re-run it until it is green. What is the main damage?
options: None; re-running is a normal workflow
Trust in the pipeline erodes, so real failures get re-run and ignored too
It only wastes compute cost
It makes test coverage go down
questions.explanation: Flaky tests teach people to ignore red builds, which defeats continuous testing. Cost matters but is secondary; coverage numbers are unchanged.

questions.prompt: Why is a defect found in a requirements review usually cheaper to fix than the same defect found in system testing?
options: Because reviewers are paid less than testers
Because nothing has yet been designed, coded, tested or documented on top of the wrong requirement
Because system testing tools are expensive
It is not cheaper; cost is the same at every stage
questions.explanation: The later a defect is found, the more work has been built on it and must be redone. That rework, not salaries or tool cost, is why early detection is cheaper.

questions.prompt: A team says: 'We shifted left with 2,000 unit tests, so we can turn off production error alerts.' What is the best response?
options: Agree; unit tests cover everything alerts would catch
Disagree: shift-left reduces defects but cannot catch production-only issues such as real traffic, configuration and third-party failures, so shift-right monitoring is still needed
Agree, but only after reaching 100% code coverage
Disagree, because unit tests are not real testing
questions.explanation: Shift-left and shift-right complement each other. Real users, data and infrastructure reveal failures no pre-release test can. Code coverage does not change that, and unit tests are certainly real testing.

questions.prompt: A pipeline runs 600 UI end-to-end tests on every commit. Analysis shows 450 of them only check input validation rules on single forms. What is the best redesign?
options: Keep all 600 but run them at night only
Move the validation checks down to unit/API level, keep a small UI end-to-end set for critical journeys, and run the broad suite less often
Delete the 450 tests
Add more machines so all 600 run faster on every commit
questions.explanation: Validation rules are cheapest and most reliable to check below the UI. Keeping the coverage at the right layer preserves safety while cutting feedback time. Deleting loses coverage; nightly only or more hardware leaves the slow, brittle layer doing work it is bad at.
